title: The Power Pose That Did Not Hold
text:
In 2010 Dana Carney, Amy Cuddy and Andy Yap reported a small experiment with a big promise. Participants held either expansive, open postures, such as leaning back with feet up on a desk, or closed, contracted postures, for about two minutes. Saliva samples were taken before and after.

According to the paper, people who struck the expansive poses showed a rise in testosterone and a drop in the stress hormone cortisol, felt more powerful and were more willing to take a gamble. The finding spread far beyond psychology. Cuddy's 2012 TED talk on power posing became one of the most watched talks ever, and many people began striking poses before interviews and presentations.

Then the evidence weakened. In 2015 a team led by Eva Ranehill ran a much larger replication and found no effect on hormones or risk taking, though people did report feeling slightly more powerful. In 2016 Dana Carney, the paper's first author, publicly stated that she no longer believed the effects were real and described problems in how the original data had been analyzed.
lesson: Be wary of quick tricks that promise instant confidence. Real authority grows from preparation, competence and practice.
people: Dana Carney, Amy Cuddy, Andy Yap
location: Columbia University and Harvard University, USA
source: Carney, D. R., Cuddy, A. J. C., and Yap, A. J. (2010). Power posing: Brief nonverbal displays affect neuroendocrine levels and risk tolerance. Psychological Science, 21(10), 1363-1368.
caveat: The hormone and risk taking effects failed to replicate and the first author disowned them; only a small effect on feeling powerful has some support.
